newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FIGURE SKATING-SOME STARS MAY MISS NAGANO OLYMPICS.
newsitem.headline: FIGURE SKATING-SOME STARS MAY MISS NAGANO OLYMPICS.

text.p: Some figure skating stars seem certain to miss next year's Olympics because of ill-considered rules brought in by the International Skating Union (ISU).

The world championships which ended at the weekend ensured that there will be enticing showdowns like those of the past when the skating protagonists gather at the Nagano Winter Games in Japan next February.
But not all the skaters who should be there will be, because of clumsy qualifying regulations voted in by the ISU's congress last June.
Because the congress is biennial, the regulations cannot be overturned until June of next year.

Yet already ISU officials are expressing regret over the fact that Russia will have only two men in the Olympics because titleholder Alexei Urmanov withdrew injured just before he was to skate in the final.
If he had been able to skate, Russia would have had three in the top six. Now those three will have to compete with others at home for just two places in Japan.

"We discussed withdrawals because of injuries but not if someone pulled out from the top group like that," Sally-Anne Stapleford of Britain, chairman of the ISU's figure skating technical committee, said on Saturday.

Under the new rule, each country accumulates points based on the placings of each of its skaters. If the total adds up to more than 21, the country can enter only two competitors in the Olympics and worlds the following year.
Any skater finishing lower than 15th, or withdrawing after the official draw is made, gets 16 points.

ISU vice-president Lawrence Demmy had earlier conceded that the qualifying points system was flawed and was being "abused and manipulated by some countries to facilitate increased representation next year, especially at the Olympics."
Demmy was referring to the fact that some countries did not bring their full entitlement of skaters to the Lausanne worlds because they could have cut their Olympic representation by doing so.
"Congress passed the rule by the two-thirds majority but nobody thought it through to foresee it being manipulated for the following year," he said.
Ukraine pulled entries out of three events here. "We must think about the Olympic Games," said their figure skating president, Ludmila Mikhailovskaya, who is also a technical committee member.
"They did not realise we could do this. The system is good for small countries but not for big countries," she added.
The United States are also down to two men for the Olympics but that was because one of their skaters, Dan Hollander, did not survive the qualifying round.
Under the Olympic qualifying system, that gave the Americans too many points to have three skaters next year.

China's Chen Lu, world champion in 1995 and runner-up last year, missed out on the women's final by one place in the short programme, finishing 25th because she was in poor condition following a foot injury.
But at least she has another chance in an October skate-off for countries without representation to secure one of six remaining Olympic places.

Yet Tara Lipinski and Michelle Kwan, the new and former world champions, seem poised to provide a memorable battle again in Nagano after Lipinski became the youngest-ever winner by usurping Kwan's title on Saturday.

Canadian champion Elvis Stojko and ex-champion Todd Eldredge have set up a confrontation to rival the "Battle of the Brians" - Orser and Boitano, which Boitano won - in 1988 and whichever two Russians qualify should provide added spice.
In the pairs, Germans Mandy Woetzel and Ingo Steuer, having secured their first world title, will take on the might of Russia once again.
In dance, the pursuit of Oksana Gritschuk and Evgeny Platov will no doubt continue just as it has ever since they won the 1994 Olympic title.
Yet there were signs in Lausanne that their crowns are slipping. They received only six first-place votes from the nine judges, an indication that their rivals may be catching up.
